title: FARM: Fundamental Agentic Reward Model For Multi-task Wireless Network Optimization

paper.title:
FARM: Fundamental Agentic Reward Model For
Multi-task Wireless Network Optimization
paper.abstract:
Abstract Future wireless networks require learning agents to adapt across heterogeneous
channel conditions, traffic patterns, quality-of-service (QoS) requirements,
objectives, and operational constraints. Reusing decision knowledge across
such tasks is challenging because conventional multi-task and transfer
reinforcement learning methods primarily share or transfer policies, coupling
transferable knowledge with task-dependent action mappings. This paper
proposes FARM (Fundamental Agentic Reward Model for Multi-task Wireless
Network Optimization), a reward-space transfer framework that shifts
cross-task knowledge reuse from policy space to trajectory-level decision
evaluation. FARM introduces an Agentic Reward Model (ARM) that learns a
task-conditioned reward prior from heterogeneous source-task trajectories and
provides auxiliary guidance for task-specific policy optimization. In Stage I,
ARM jointly models task conditions, temporal trajectory dependencies, and
objective-dependent reward structures while each source task retains its own
controller. In Stage II, the learned reward prior is frozen and reused to guide
the adaptation of a target-specific controller for previously unseen tasks,
without transferring source-task policies. Experiments on heterogeneous multi-access edge computing
(MEC) tasks show that FARM achieves a mean late-stage gain of 29.8 % 29.8\% over Single-task SAC on unseen Rate–Latency targets,
compared with 16.1 % 16.1\% for CRA Transfer, and reaches a 46.2 % 46.2\% gain on the moderate-OOD FAR-M case.
Further analysis shows that both Mamba and Transformer trajectory encoders
support Reward-Space Transfer, while Mamba provides improved robustness
as longer history dependencies are introduced.

Ma is with Tencent Hunyuan Frontier Lab, Singapore (email: haozhe.ma@u.nus.edu) Abstract Future wireless networks require learning agents to adapt across heterogeneous channel conditions, traffic patterns, quality-of-service (QoS) requirements, objectives, and operational constraints. Reusing decision knowledge across such tasks is challenging because conventional multi-task and transfer reinforcement learning methods primarily share or transfer policies, coupling transferable knowledge with task-dependent action mappings. This paper proposes FARM (Fundamental Agentic Reward Model for Multi-task Wireless Network Optimization), a reward-space transfer framework that shifts cross-task knowledge reuse from policy space to trajectory-level decision evaluation. FARM introduces an Agentic Reward Model (ARM) that learns a task-conditioned reward prior from heterogeneous source-task trajectories and provides auxiliary guidance for task-specific policy optimization. In Stage I, ARM jointly models task conditions, temporal trajectory dependencies, and objective-dependent reward structures while each source task retains its own controller. In Stage II, the learned reward prior is frozen and reused to guide the adaptation of a target-specific controller for previously unseen tasks, without transferring source-task policies. Experiments on heterogeneous multi-access edge computing (MEC) tasks show that FARM achieves a mean late-stage gain of 29.8 % 29.8\% over Single-task SAC on unseen Rate–Latency targets, compared with 16.1 % 16.1\% for CRA Transfer, and reaches a 46.2 % 46.2\% gain on the moderate-OOD FAR-M case. Further analysis shows that both Mamba and Transformer trajectory encoders support Reward-Space Transfer, while Mamba provides improved robustness as longer history dependencies are introduced. Index Terms: Intelligent wireless networks, reinforcement learning, reward-space transfer, reward representation learning I Introduction Future wireless networks are evolving from isolated optimization systems toward intelligent and autonomous platforms, where learning-enabled agents must continuously adapt their decisions to dynamic and heterogeneous environments [ 1 ] . Unlike conventional wireless optimization, which typically assumes a predefined objective under a fixed system configuration, future networks must accommodate diverse users, services, and operational requirements under varying channel conditions, traffic patterns, quality-of-service (QoS) preferences, and optimization objectives [ 2 ] . Multi-access edge computing (MEC) provides a representative setting for such intelligent wireless control, where communication, computation, and energy resources must be jointly optimized under complex and time-varying conditions [ 3 ] . Accordingly, future wireless intelligence requires not only effective decision-making for individual tasks, but also the ability to acquire and reuse optimization knowledge across heterogeneous tasks. Instead of independently learning a controller for every task, scalable wireless intelligence requires mechanisms that can reuse and adapt optimization knowledge across related yet distinct task distributions [ 4 ] . These tasks may differ in channel statistics, traffic patterns, QoS priorities, constraint configurations, and optimization preferences, such as throughput maximization, latency reduction, energy minimization, or their combinations. Effective cross-task knowledge reuse therefore becomes a central challenge for intelligent wireless networks. Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has demonstrated strong capability for adaptive wireless optimization through interaction with dynamic environments [ 5 ] . However, most existing DRL approaches remain task specific, with learned policies closely coupled to particular environments, objectives, and action mappings. Multi-task reinforcement learning (MT-RL) and transfer learning improve knowledge reuse primarily through policy sharing or policy transfer. Although effective for related tasks, such policy representations inherently entangle reusable optimization knowledge with task-dependent action generation. When channel statistics, objectives, QoS requirements, or constraints change, transferred policies may retain source-specific control patterns and require substantial adaptation. This coupling can introduce cross-task interference and limit the scalability of policy-level transfer under heterogeneous wireless conditions. This limitation motivates a fundamental question: what should be transferred across heterogeneous wireless optimization tasks? Therefore, we investigate reward representations as an alternative interface for cross-task knowledge reuse. Our key premise is that, although optimal actions may differ substantially across tasks, the principles used to evaluate decision trajectories can exhibit stronger cross-task regularities. Such trajectory-level evaluation knowledge captures how sequences of observations and actions contribute to long-term optimization objectives under different wireless conditions without directly specifying a task-dependent action mapping. This observation motivates Reward-Space Transfer , in which transferable reward representations are learned from heterogeneous interaction trajectories and reused as auxiliary guidance for task-specific policy optimization. Realizing effective Reward-Space Transfer raises three key challenges. First, heterogeneous wireless tasks have different evaluation semantics due to variations in optimization objectives, QoS requirements, channel conditions, and constraints. The same trajectory may therefore have different utility under different task contexts, requiring reward evaluation to be explicitly conditioned on task characteristics. Second, reward learning must balance cross-task commonality and task-specific specialization: a fully shared representation may suppress objective-dependent preferences, whereas independent reward models eliminate the benefit of knowledge reuse. Third, reward knowledge learned from source tasks must remain useful under unseen task configurations. Since target tasks may introduce new combinations of channel dynamics, QoS requirements, objectives, and constraints, transfer must selectively exploit relevant prior knowledge while avoiding mismatched reward guidance under distribution shift. To address these challenges, we propose FARM, a Fundamental Agentic Reward Model for multi-task wireless network optimization, as illustrated in Fig. 1 . FARM shifts the transferable component from task-specific policies to trajectory-level decision evaluation knowledge. Its core component, the Agentic Reward Model (ARM), learns a transferable reward prior from heterogeneous wireless interaction trajectories. Importantly, the learned reward does not replace the original task objective; instead, it provides auxiliary guidance that complements the environment reward during task-specific policy optimization. FARM therefore separates reusable reward knowledge from task-dependent action generation while allowing individual controllers to remain specialized to their corresponding wireless environments. FARM follows a two-stage learning and transfer paradigm. In Stage I, ARM learns a transferable reward prior from a heterogeneous source-task bank by jointly modeling task conditions, temporal trajectory dependencies, and objective-dependent reward structures, while each source task retains its own controller. In Stage II, the learned reward prior is frozen and reused for previously unseen target tasks without transferring source-task policies. Objective-aware routing and task-conditioned reward generation provide auxiliary guidance, while the target-specific controller is optimized using the original environment reward together with the transferred reward signal. To support task-aware reward reasoning, ARM combines a task-condition interface for channel configurations, optimization preferences, QoS requirements, and constraints with a trajectory representation module over historical observations, actions, and rewards. Condition-aware feature modulation and objective-specific reward experts reconcile shared reward knowledge with task-dependent evaluation semantics, while adaptive auxiliary-reward weighting controls the contribution of transferred guidance. A Mamba-based selective state-space encoder is adopted as the default temporal backbone to capture long-range dependencies in dynamic wireless environments. Together, these components enable ARM to learn reusable trajectory-level reward knowledge while preserving the task specificity required for heterogeneous wireless optimization. The main contributions of this paper are as follows: • We introduce FARM, a Fundamental Agentic Reward Modeling framework that formulates Reward-Space Transfer for heterogeneous wireless optimization. Unlike policy sharing or policy transfer, FARM transfers trajectory-level decision evaluation knowledge and uses the learned reward prior as auxiliary guidance for task-specific policy optimization, thereby decoupling transferable knowledge from task-dependent action mappings. • We develop ARM for learning transferable reward representations from heterogeneous wireless trajectories. ARM integrates task-condition encoding, temporal trajectory modeling, condition-aware feature modulation, objective-specific reward experts, and adaptive auxiliary-reward weighting to capture reusable evaluation knowledge across tasks while retaining task-specific objective and constraint information. • We design a two-stage reward-space learning and transfer mechanism in which a transferable reward prior is learned from heterogeneous source tasks and subsequently reused on unseen target tasks while the shared reward prior remains frozen. Objective-aware routing and task-conditioned reward guidance support target-policy adaptation under distribution shifts. Experiments on heterogeneous MEC tasks demonstrate effective multi-task reward learning and Reward-Space Transfer to unseen tasks, while temporal-backbone analysis shows that Mamba provides improved robustness when longer history dependencies are introduced. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section II discusses related work. Section III presents the system model. Section IV gives the problem formulation. Section V details the design of the algorithm. Section VI presents experimental results and analysis. Finally, Section VII concludes the paper with a summary of our key findings. Fig. 1: Overview of heterogeneous wireless tasks considered by FARM. The task space spans diverse channel conditions, QoS objectives, constraints, and deployment scenarios. (I) Rayleigh fading models dense urban and mobile MEC environments with rapid non-line-of-sight variations. (II) Rician fading represents line-of-sight-dominant UAV-assisted and air-ground MEC scenarios. (III) Nakagami- m m fading captures adjustable propagation severity in V2X and industrial robotic environments.
